_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 8 Mixtures. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (a mixture; the sieve; the magnet; the filter; dissolving; risks), in the lesson's own words and with its own things: its sand and stones, the kit's sieve drawing, its iron filings and magnet, its filter paper and funnel, its salt and water, and the safe and risky items of its Safe scientist step.
title: Mixtures
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Understand that a mixture contains two or more materials, where the materials can be physically separated.
Understand that materials, generally, retain their properties within a mixture.
Describe how to separate solid/solid mixtures based on the physical properties of the solids (processes involving dissolving are not required).
Describe how to separate a mixture of an insoluble solid and a liquid.
Know that when a solid dissolves in a liquid the solid is still present, and this is an example of mixing.
Identify risks and explain how to stay safe during practical work.

beats.say: Mix sand and stones together in a bowl. That is a mixture.
Two materials in one place, and each one stays exactly itself.
Here is sand. Fine grains that pour through your fingers.
Here are stones. Big and hard. They do not pour at all.
Mix them in a bowl. That is a mixture: two materials together.
You might think that mixing makes one new material. It does not.
Look closely. The sand is still sand, the stones still stones.
Nothing changed. Each material keeps its own properties.
Each material kept its properties, so you can get them apart.
Sand and stones are very different sizes. So use a sieve.
Shake it. The fine sand falls straight through the holes.
The stones are too big and stay behind. Separated by size.
Iron filings and sand are both tiny. A sieve cannot help.
But only the iron is magnetic. Sweep a magnet over them.
The filings jump onto the magnet. The sand is left behind.
Careful: not every metal is magnetic. Iron and steel are; copper wire is not.
Sand in water is a mixture too. Both of them are still there.

at.both: Both of them are still there

beats.say: Put a funnel over a jug. Line it with filter paper. Pour it slowly.
The water drips through into the jug below, and it is clear.
The sand cannot get through the tiny holes. It stays behind.
A funnel only guides the liquid. The paper does the separating.
Now stir a spoon of salt into water. Watch it disappear.
Has the salt gone for ever? No. It is still there.
Taste one drop, with a grown-up. The water is salty.
So the salt is still in the glass, in pieces too small to see.
Dissolving is a kind of mixing. It is not a vanishing.
Salt and sugar dissolve. Sand and pebbles do not.
Practical work has risks. A risk is something that could hurt someone.
Glass can break. Floors get wet. Some powders can hurt you.
A scientist spots the risks first: goggles on, spills wiped.
Hair tied back. And taste nothing unless a grown-up says it is safe.
A mixture holds two materials, and each keeps its properties.
A sieve separates by size. A magnet pulls the iron out of the sand.
A filter holds the sand back and lets the water through.
Dissolved salt is still there. And a scientist spots the risks.
